doc.title: Herb Ellis interviewed by Michael Woods, Los Angeles, California, September 3, 1995 [interview 1 of 2]

title: Accompanying Ella Fitzgerald and singers; the rhythm section beat
summary: Ellis describes following Ella through verses and tugging singers who lag the beat, then how drums, bass, piano and guitar should sit together.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Great drummers: who they admired and why

blocks.x: Now you played some behind Ella Fitzgerald. How is it different to accompany a singer, especially a great singer?

Oh and she is the greatest. Ella, for instance when she was singing the verse to a tune, out of time you know, and you’re playing for her, you just kind of have to tag after her. Because she goes right through it — bang you know. Now somebody like, oh I can’t © Fillius Jazz Archive -4-

think of the names but it doesn’t matter, maybe I’ll think of it later, sing way behind the beat. I mean way behind the beat. You’ve got to be tugging them, like with a rope you know. Not that it’s bad, it’s just that you have to learn how to do with each singer.
About the time element, this tugging feeling, that is an essential part of jazz. Can you kind of describe that?
As you know for instance with a lead player either pushing ahead on the beat or pulling behind as compared to the rhythm section.

Oh, I see. Well in my opinion the rhythm section sounds best when the drummer plays right on the beat, and the bass is just a hair on top of that. Not enough that you get a [claps]. It’s just a little edge. That’s the way Ray Brown plays and other players too. And then the pianist, they just have to know what to leave out, and the guitarist has to learn how to play with the rhythm section but with the pianist. That’s the thing. So you don’t get in each other’s way you know. So that’s the way an optimum rhythm section would work for me. That’s the optimum way it would work I mean to say.
